newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel approves food-stamp privatization.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel approves food-stamp privatization.

text.p: States would be allowed to hire contractors to run part of the food stamp program under language approved Thursday by the House Agriculture Committee.

Lawmakers voted 24-19 in favor of the provision before approving legislation to allow an additional $1.5 billion to be spent through the food stamp program on job training and hardship exemptions from limits on aid to able-bodied people.
Food stamps are the major U.S. antihunger program, helping more than 20 million poor people a month buy groceries.

Representative Larry Combest, Texas Republican and author of the amendment, said his state could save $10 million if it could hire private contractors to determine if applicants were eligible for food stamps. The Clinton administration has rejected the state's request to do so as part of welfare reform.
"We have had absolute, total opposition to do anything," said Representative Charles Stenholm, Texas Democrat, in explaining why congressional action was sought.

Only one Democrat joined Stenholm in voting for the proposal while Republicans uniformly voted for it. Most Democrats called the Texas proposal untested and unlikely to actually save any money but certain to displace government workers with outsiders.
"It was a Texas thing. Think about it," Agriculture Committee Cairman Bob Smith said afterward when asked about the party line Republican support for the plan.

Two of the top-ranking Republicans in the House, Texans Dick Armey and Tom DeLay, signed a letter asking colleagues to support the plan. Ohioan John Boehner, No 4 in Republican leadership, also signed the letter.

The legislation will be wrapped into a so-called budget reconciliation bill to carry out terms of the balanced budget pact passed by Congress. The Senate Agriculture Committee approved the additional $1.5 billion in spending earlier this week but did not consider any amendments.

During its session, the House Agriculture Committee rejected, 30-13, a Stenholm amemdnent to cap the amount of money given to states for running the food stamp program. The White House, governors and legislators opposed the amendment.

Stenholm said a loophole in last year's welfare reform law allowed states to inflate their spending. He said the cap would save $1.67 billion through 2002. He proposed using the money for several programs, including more money for a food assistance program.

Most of the reallocated money would have gone to items aiding farmers. They included extending the life of the Fund for Rural America through 2002, making so-called Step 2 cotton payments available even if special import quotas are in effect, giving barley growers an additional $30 million, and helping cover the cost of the federal crop insurance program.
